modules.title: Java Basics
modules.summary: Understand variables, operators, conditions and loops.
notes: Java is statically typed, so variables have declared types such as int, double and String.
Control statements include if/else, switch, for, while and do-while.
The main method is the common starting point of a standalone Java program.

concepts.title: Program structure
concepts.text: A Java application is built from classes. A standalone program normally begins in public static void main(String[] args). Source files are compiled by javac into JVM bytecode, then the java launcher executes that bytecode through the Java Virtual Machine.

concepts.title: Types and variables
concepts.text: Java is statically typed. Primitive types include int, double, boolean and char; reference types include String, arrays and user-defined classes. The compiler checks assignments and method calls against these declared types before the program runs.

concepts.title: Operators and decisions
concepts.text: Arithmetic and comparison operators build expressions, while &&, || and ! combine boolean conditions. if/else handles general decisions and switch is useful for exact alternatives. Strings should be compared by content with equals(), not with ==.

concepts.title: Loops
concepts.text: for loops are useful when the iteration pattern is known, while and do-while repeat based on a condition, and enhanced for loops traverse arrays or collections directly. Casting may be required when an arithmetic expression would otherwise use integer division.

codeExample.title: Simple Java program
explanation: The enhanced for loop reads every array value.
Casting total to double prevents integer division.
The compiler checks the declared types before execution.

diagram.title: Java execution path
diagram.caption: Java separates source compilation from bytecode execution, which is why the same bytecode can run on different systems with a compatible JVM.

applications: Console utilities, backend services and object-oriented applications all begin with the same type and control-flow fundamentals.
commonMistakes: Comparing String values with ==.
Performing integer division accidentally.
Using an uninitialized local variable.
Creating non-terminating loops.
bestPractices: Let compiler errors guide corrections early.

modules.title: Classes & OOP
modules.summary: Model data and behavior with objects and classes.
notes: A class defines fields and methods, while an object is an instance of that class.
Encapsulation hides internal data behind controlled methods.
Inheritance and polymorphism support reusable and flexible object-oriented designs.

concepts.title: Classes and objects
concepts.text: A class is a blueprint containing fields and methods; an object is a particular instance created from that blueprint. Constructors initialize a new instance and should establish a valid starting state.

concepts.title: Encapsulation
concepts.text: Encapsulation keeps fields private and exposes controlled behaviour through methods. Instead of letting any code assign arbitrary values, the class can validate changes and protect its own invariants.

concepts.title: Inheritance and composition
concepts.text: Inheritance models a true 'is-a' specialization, while composition models 'has-a' collaboration. Composition is often more flexible because one object can delegate work to another without creating a deep type hierarchy.

concepts.title: Polymorphism and abstraction
concepts.text: Interfaces and parent types let different concrete objects be used through one contract. When an overridden method is invoked, Java dispatches to the implementation belonging to the actual runtime object.

codeExample.title: Encapsulated learner
explanation: The fields are private.
Callers can change state only through meaningful methods.
The constructor guarantees every learner starts with a name.

diagram.title: OOP model
diagram.caption: Objects combine state and behaviour, while abstraction controls how other parts of the program interact with them.

applications: Learners, courses, reports and notification strategies can all be modeled as objects with clear responsibilities.
commonMistakes: Making all fields public.
Using inheritance only for code reuse.
Creating deep class hierarchies.
Forgetting @Override on intended overrides.
bestPractices: Prefer composition unless inheritance expresses a real relationship.

modules.title: Collections & Exceptions
modules.summary: Work with collections and handle runtime problems safely.
notes: ArrayList stores a resizable ordered collection of elements.
HashMap stores key-value pairs for fast lookup by key.
try/catch handles exceptions so a program can recover or provide a meaningful error.

concepts.title: List, Set and Map
concepts.text: List preserves order and allows duplicates, Set represents unique values, and Map associates keys with values. Common implementations include ArrayList, HashSet and HashMap. Code often declares variables using the interface type so the implementation can change later.

concepts.title: Generics and iteration
concepts.text: Generic type parameters such as List<String> provide compile-time type safety. Collections can be traversed with enhanced for loops, iterators or streams. When removing during iteration, use safe mechanisms such as Iterator.remove or removeIf.

concepts.title: Exceptions
concepts.text: Exceptions represent abnormal conditions. try contains work that may fail, catch handles a matching exception, and finally is used for cleanup logic that must run regardless of success or failure. Catch the most specific exception you can actually handle.

concepts.title: Resource safety
concepts.text: Files, streams and JDBC objects should be closed. try-with-resources automatically closes AutoCloseable resources even when an exception occurs, which is safer than relying on manual cleanup.

codeExample.title: Collections and validation
explanation: removeIf safely filters the mutable list.
The map provides key-based lookup.
Generics ensure only the expected value types are stored.

diagram.title: Exception path
diagram.caption: Exception handling keeps recovery logic separate from the normal path and guarantees that necessary cleanup can still happen.

applications: Collections store learners, skills and scores; exception handling protects file, input and database operations.
commonMistakes: Using raw collections without generic types.
Catching Exception and ignoring it.
Modifying a collection unsafely while iterating.
Forgetting to close resources.

modules.title: Node.js Runtime & Modules
modules.summary: Understand Node.js, CommonJS/ES modules and npm.
notes: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser using the V8 engine.
Modules split applications into reusable files and npm manages project dependencies.
package.json describes scripts, metadata and dependencies for a Node.js project.

concepts.title: What Node.js provides
concepts.text: Node.js uses the V8 JavaScript engine and adds runtime APIs for files, networking, processes and the operating system. That allows JavaScript to build servers and command-line tools outside the browser.

concepts.title: The process object
concepts.text: process exposes environment variables, command-line arguments, the current working directory and exit information. Server configuration such as ports and database credentials should come from the environment rather than being hard-coded into source files.

concepts.title: Modules
concepts.text: CommonJS uses require() and module.exports, while ES modules use import/export when the project is configured for them. Modules split a program into focused files with explicit public interfaces.

concepts.title: npm and dependencies
concepts.text: package.json records scripts, metadata and dependencies. package-lock.json pins the exact dependency tree for repeatable installs. Packages should be added deliberately because every dependency increases maintenance and security surface.

codeExample.title: CommonJS module
explanation: One file exports a small public API.
Another file imports only the function it needs.
Node caches loaded CommonJS modules after resolution.

diagram.title: Node runtime
diagram.caption: Node combines V8 with server-side APIs that are not normally available to browser JavaScript.

applications: Express servers, command-line utilities, automation scripts and build tools all run on Node.js.
commonMistakes: Hard-coding secrets.
Mixing module systems without understanding configuration.
Installing packages for trivial built-in functionality.
Ignoring lockfiles.

modules.title: Async JavaScript & Event Loop
modules.summary: Use promises, async/await and non-blocking I/O.
notes: The event loop coordinates asynchronous callbacks so the main thread can remain responsive.
Promises represent future success or failure and async/await provides readable promise syntax.
Long CPU-heavy synchronous work can block other requests.

concepts.title: Non-blocking I/O
concepts.text: Node.js can start many I/O operations without waiting synchronously for each one to finish. While the operating system or runtime waits on network/file operations, the JavaScript thread can continue handling other ready work.

concepts.title: Promises
concepts.text: A Promise represents a future result and can be pending, fulfilled or rejected. then/catch can consume that result; Promise.all is useful when independent operations can safely run concurrently.

concepts.title: async/await
concepts.text: async functions return Promises, and await pauses only the current async function until a Promise settles. It does not block the whole Node process. try/catch provides natural error handling around awaited operations.

concepts.title: The event loop
concepts.text: The event loop schedules ready JavaScript callbacks and promise continuations. Asynchronous I/O improves concurrency, but CPU-heavy synchronous work still blocks the event loop because JavaScript callbacks need the main thread.

codeExample.title: Concurrent async operations
explanation: Both independent operations start before either result is awaited.
Promise.all fails if one member rejects.
The caller still receives one Promise from the async function.

diagram.title: Simplified event loop
diagram.caption: Asynchronous I/O frees the JavaScript thread while waiting, but the continuation still runs only when the event loop can schedule it.

applications: Database queries, file operations and HTTP requests should use asynchronous APIs in a web server.
commonMistakes: Assuming async/await creates a thread per request.
Forgetting rejected Promise handling.
Awaiting independent operations serially.
Running CPU-heavy loops in request handlers.
bestPractices: Run independent tasks concurrently where safe.

modules.title: HTTP Servers
modules.summary: Handle requests and responses using Node.js HTTP concepts.
notes: HTTP requests contain a method, URL, headers and sometimes a body.
HTTP responses contain a status code, headers and optional response body.
Frameworks such as Express reduce routing and middleware boilerplate.

concepts.title: HTTP request/response
concepts.text: A client sends a method, URL, headers and optionally a body. The server returns a status code, headers and optionally a response body. Node's http module exposes these protocol details directly.

concepts.title: Methods and status codes
concepts.text: GET retrieves, POST commonly creates or triggers processing, PUT/PATCH update and DELETE removes. Status codes such as 200, 201, 400, 401, 404 and 500 communicate the outcome independently of response text.

concepts.title: Bodies and JSON
concepts.text: Incoming request bodies arrive as chunks at the low level. A server collects them and parses JSON after the stream ends. Frameworks such as Express automate this repetitive parsing through middleware.

concepts.title: Headers and CORS
concepts.text: Content-Type describes the representation. Cookies carry session identifiers. When frontend and backend origins differ, browser CORS rules determine whether JavaScript can access the response; credentialed requests require explicit allowed origins.

codeExample.title: Minimal Node HTTP server
explanation: The method and path form a very small route.
Every response includes an appropriate status and content type.
Unmatched requests receive a 404.

diagram.title: HTTP lifecycle
diagram.caption: Every REST API call follows this request/response lifecycle even when a framework hides the low-level details.

applications: Health checks and REST APIs are built on the same HTTP primitives.
commonMistakes: Sending a response twice.
Using 200 for errors.
Trusting JSON without validation.
Using unsafe credentialed CORS settings.
bestPractices: Understand HTTP before relying on framework helpers.

modules.title: HTML Structure
modules.summary: Build semantic pages with common HTML elements.
notes: HTML gives a web page its structure using elements such as headings, paragraphs, links, images and forms.
Semantic elements such as header, nav, main, section and footer improve readability and accessibility.
Attributes provide extra information such as href for links, src for images and type for form controls.

concepts.title: Document structure
concepts.text: A modern HTML document begins with a doctype, then uses the html element as the root. The head stores metadata such as the character set, viewport information and page title, while the body contains the visible interface. Correct nesting matters because the browser converts this markup into a document tree that CSS and JavaScript later use.

concepts.title: Elements and attributes
concepts.text: HTML elements describe content such as headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists and forms. Attributes configure those elements: href identifies a link destination, src identifies a resource, alt describes meaningful images, and type changes the behaviour of an input. Good markup chooses the element that best describes the content rather than using generic containers for everything.

concepts.title: Semantic HTML
concepts.text: Semantic elements such as header, nav, main, section, article, aside and footer communicate the role of each region. They improve maintainability and provide landmarks that assistive technologies can use. Semantic HTML does not mean replacing every div; use a generic container when no element has a more accurate meaning.

concepts.title: Forms and accessibility
concepts.text: Forms should pair every control with a meaningful label and use input types that match the data being collected. Native buttons, links, labels and headings already contain useful keyboard and accessibility behaviour. Starting with correct HTML usually produces a more robust interface than rebuilding basic controls with generic div elements.

codeExample.title: Semantic page example
codeExample.code:
SkillForge

Continue learning

Resume your current course.

© SkillForge
explanation: The document declares its language and viewport before visible content begins.
Semantic regions describe the purpose of each major area.
Headings follow a logical hierarchy and links are used for navigation.

diagram.title: Semantic page hierarchy
diagram.caption: A browser reads the document as a hierarchy. Semantic regions make that hierarchy understandable to developers and assistive tools.

applications: Landing pages, course pages, forms, dashboards and articles all begin with sound document structure.
commonMistakes: Using div for every region even when a semantic element fits better.
Skipping heading levels for visual styling reasons.
Using placeholder text instead of a persistent form label.
Omitting alt text from meaningful images.
bestPractices: Write the HTML structure before styling it.
Use one clear main content area.

modules.title: CSS Styling
modules.summary: Use selectors, the box model and reusable style rules.
notes: CSS selectors choose which HTML elements a rule will style.
The box model contains content, padding, border and margin.
Classes are reusable and are usually preferred over styling many elements with unique IDs.

concepts.title: Selectors and the cascade
concepts.text: CSS rules target elements with selectors and assign visual properties. Several rules may match the same element, so the cascade considers origin, importance, specificity and source order. Reusable class selectors are usually easier to maintain than deeply nested or highly specific selectors.

concepts.title: The box model
concepts.text: Every rendered element behaves like a rectangular box containing content, padding, border and margin. Padding creates space inside the border, while margin creates space outside it. Using box-sizing: border-box makes declared width and height include padding and border, which usually makes sizing more predictable.

concepts.title: Typography and design tokens
concepts.text: Readable interfaces depend on font size, line height, contrast and spacing. CSS custom properties can hold repeated values such as brand colors, surface colors, border radii and spacing. This creates a small design system and makes dark/light theme changes easier.

concepts.title: Interaction states
concepts.text: Interactive components should communicate hover, focus, active and disabled states. Pointer hover is helpful, but keyboard users rely on visible focus styles, so focus outlines should not be removed without an accessible replacement. Short transitions can make state changes feel smoother without distracting from the content.

codeExample.title: Reusable card styling
explanation: Custom properties centralize the important visual values.
border-box keeps component dimensions easier to calculate.
The hover change is small enough to signal interactivity without moving the layout dramatically.

diagram.title: CSS box model
diagram.caption: The four layers wrap from outside to inside. Understanding which layer creates space makes layout debugging much faster.

applications: Cards, forms, navigation, dashboards and responsive components all depend on predictable CSS rules.
commonMistakes: Using fixed widths plus padding without understanding box sizing.
Overusing !important.
Removing keyboard focus indicators.
Using low-contrast text colors.
bestPractices: Define common colors and spacing once.
Test keyboard focus as well as hover.
Keep selectors as simple as the component allows.

modules.title: Layouts & Responsive Design
modules.summary: Create flexible layouts using Flexbox, Grid and media queries.
notes: Flexbox is useful for one-dimensional row or column layouts.
CSS Grid is useful for two-dimensional page layouts.
Media queries adapt layouts to different screen widths and are a core part of responsive design.

concepts.title: Fluid foundations
concepts.text: Responsive design starts with flexible widths, max-width constraints, relative units and content that can wrap. A layout should naturally adapt before a media query is added. Functions such as min(), max() and clamp() help values scale within sensible limits.

concepts.title: Flexbox
concepts.text: Flexbox arranges items along one main axis and is useful for navigation rows, button groups and aligned card content. justify-content controls distribution on the main axis, align-items controls the cross axis, and flex-wrap lets items move to additional lines when space becomes limited.

concepts.title: CSS Grid
concepts.text: Grid manages rows and columns together, which makes it well suited to dashboards and card galleries. repeat(), minmax() and auto-fit can create responsive layouts that automatically add or remove columns as available width changes.

concepts.title: Media queries
concepts.text: Media queries should solve actual layout failures rather than target a long list of device models. A mobile-first approach starts with the simplest narrow layout and adds enhancements when more space becomes available. Responsive design also considers touch targets, text zoom and user preferences such as reduced motion.

codeExample.title: Responsive card grid
explanation: The grid chooses the number of columns automatically.
Cards never become narrower than 240px.
The page remains centered and leaves safe side spacing on smaller screens.

diagram.title: Responsive workflow
diagram.caption: Responsive design is iterative: start fluid, observe where content fails, then add the smallest required adjustment.

applications: Course catalogs, dashboards, authentication pages and learning workspaces need to remain usable on many viewport sizes.
commonMistakes: Creating device-specific layouts for every common phone size.
Using absolute positioning for major page structure.
Giving cards fixed widths that force horizontal scrolling.
Testing only one mobile and one desktop width.
bestPractices: Use Grid/Flexbox before reaching for position hacks.
Test long labels and zoomed text.

modules.title: Variables & Control Flow
modules.summary: Use variables, data types, operators and decisions.
notes: let and const declare block-scoped variables; const prevents reassignment of the variable binding.
JavaScript supports values such as strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, objects, null and undefined.
if/else and switch select code paths, while loops repeat work.

concepts.title: Variables and values
concepts.text: JavaScript stores values in variables declared with const or let. const prevents reassignment of the binding, while let is appropriate when the value must change. JavaScript is dynamically typed, so the type belongs to the current value rather than being permanently attached to the variable.

concepts.title: Data types and operators
concepts.text: Primitive values include strings, numbers, booleans, undefined, null, bigint and symbol. Objects, arrays and functions are reference values. Arithmetic, comparison and logical operators combine these values into expressions; strict equality (===) is normally preferred because it does not perform implicit type coercion.

concepts.title: Conditional logic
concepts.text: if, else if and else select one branch based on boolean conditions. switch is useful when one expression is compared with several exact values. Clear conditions are easier to maintain when complex tests are stored in descriptively named variables instead of being repeated inline.

concepts.title: Loops
concepts.text: for, while, do...while and for...of repeat work. for...of is especially readable for arrays when the index is not needed. Every loop must make progress toward termination; otherwise it can block the page or server with an infinite loop.

explanation: The conditions are evaluated from top to bottom.

diagram.caption: Control flow determines which statements execute and which are skipped.

applications: Form validation, quiz scoring, progress calculations and UI state all use variables and control flow.

Reassigning a const variable.

Creating a loop whose condition never changes.

modules.title: Functions, Arrays & Objects
modules.summary: Organize logic with functions and collections.
notes: Functions package reusable behavior and can receive parameters and return values.
Arrays store ordered values and provide methods such as map, filter and find.
Objects group related data using key-value properties.

concepts.title: Functions
concepts.text: Functions package reusable behaviour. Parameters describe incoming data, arguments are the actual values passed by a caller, and return sends a result back. Small functions with clear inputs and outputs are easier to test and reuse than large procedures that read and mutate many global values.

concepts.title: Arrays
concepts.text: Arrays store ordered values and provide methods for common transformations. map creates a new array by transforming every item, filter keeps items matching a condition, find returns the first match, and reduce combines the collection into one accumulated result.

concepts.title: Objects
concepts.text: Objects group related data under named properties, making them useful for entities such as learners, courses and quiz attempts. Dot notation is concise for known property names; bracket notation is useful when a key is computed dynamically.

concepts.title: Destructuring and spread
concepts.text: Destructuring extracts selected properties or array items into variables. Spread syntax can create a shallow copy with modified fields, which is useful when UI code should avoid mutating shared state directly.

codeExample.title: Transform course data
explanation: filter removes incomplete courses.
map then extracts only the title from each remaining object.
The original array is left unchanged.

diagram.title: Data transformation pipeline
diagram.caption: Array methods can be chained into a readable sequence of selecting, transforming and summarizing data.

applications: Dashboards commonly filter enrolled courses, map API records into cards and reduce quiz results into averages.
commonMistakes: Forgetting return in a block-bodied arrow callback.
Mutating shared objects unexpectedly.
Using map when filter or forEach better matches the intent.
Writing one large function that fetches, calculates and renders everything.
bestPractices: Use objects for named structured data.
Prefer clear transformations over hidden mutation.

modules.title: DOM & Events
modules.summary: Make pages interactive by reading and updating the DOM.
notes: The DOM represents the HTML document as objects JavaScript can query and modify.
addEventListener attaches behavior to events such as click, input and submit.
User input should be validated before it is processed or sent to a backend.

concepts.title: The DOM tree
concepts.text: The browser parses HTML into the Document Object Model, a tree of nodes exposed through the document object. JavaScript can query that tree and change the visible page without reloading the whole document.

concepts.title: Selecting and updating elements
concepts.text: querySelector returns the first element matching a CSS selector and querySelectorAll returns a collection of matches. textContent is the safest default for plain external text, while classList is useful for adding or removing state classes.

concepts.title: Events
concepts.text: Events represent user or browser actions such as click, input, submit and keydown. addEventListener attaches handlers without overwriting existing behaviour. The event object exposes the target and lets a handler prevent default browser behaviour when the application intentionally replaces it.

concepts.title: Event delegation
concepts.text: Most events bubble through ancestor elements. A parent can therefore listen for interactions from many child elements, which is especially useful for lists created dynamically after an API response. closest() helps determine whether the original target was inside an actionable control.

codeExample.title: Delegated course action
explanation: Only one listener is attached to the list.
closest() handles clicks on text or icons inside the button.
The pattern continues to work for cards inserted later.

diagram.title: DOM interaction flow
diagram.caption: The DOM is where JavaScript turns data and user actions into visible interface changes.

applications: Course-card buttons, forms, theme toggles, progress controls and quiz options all rely on DOM events.
commonMistakes: Using innerHTML with untrusted text.
Attaching duplicate listeners on every re-render.
Assuming querySelector always finds an element.
Listening only for button click when form submit is the real interaction.
bestPractices: Use event delegation for dynamic collections.

Fetch resolves for HTTP error responses too, so inspect response.ok before consuming successful data.
Use try/catch/finally to display errors and restore loading controls after either success or failure.

concepts.title: Putting it into practice

modules.title: Python Syntax & Decisions
modules.summary: Use Python variables, conditions and loops.
notes: Python uses indentation to define code blocks instead of braces.
Variables are dynamically typed and can refer to different value types.
if/elif/else handles decisions, while for and while handle repetition.

concepts.title: Readable syntax
concepts.text: Python uses indentation rather than braces to define blocks. Consistent four-space indentation is therefore part of program correctness, not only formatting.

concepts.title: Values and dynamic typing
concepts.text: Variables are created by assignment and can refer to values of different types over time. Common types include int, float, str, bool and None, while type() and isinstance() can inspect values when needed.

concepts.title: Decisions
concepts.text: if, elif and else choose branches. Python supports chained comparisons such as 0 <= score <= 100 and uses and, or and not for boolean logic. Use == for value comparison and reserve is mainly for identity checks such as value is None.

concepts.title: Loops
concepts.text: for iterates directly over iterables such as lists, ranges and strings; while repeats while a condition remains true. enumerate() provides indexes alongside values and often replaces manual counter logic.

codeExample.title: Python score classification
explanation: Indentation defines each branch.
Only the first true condition executes.
The syntax stays compact without braces.

diagram.title: Python decision flow
diagram.caption: Only one branch of an if/elif/else chain runs, after which execution continues below the block.

applications: Automation scripts, data processing and backend code all depend on these basic types and control structures.
commonMistakes: Mixing tabs and spaces.
Using is for ordinary value equality.
Shadowing built-ins such as list or str.
Writing manual index loops where direct iteration is clearer.
bestPractices: Use None explicitly for missing values.

modules.title: Functions & Collections
modules.summary: Organize code and work with lists, dictionaries and sets.
notes: def declares a function and return sends a result back to the caller.
Lists are ordered and mutable; tuples are ordered and commonly used as immutable records.
Dictionaries store values by key and are useful for structured lookup.

concepts.title: Functions and return values
concepts.text: Functions are defined with def and group reusable logic behind a name. Parameters describe the inputs and return sends a result back to the caller. A function with no explicit return produces None.

concepts.title: Lists and tuples
concepts.text: Lists are mutable ordered collections and support operations such as append, remove, slicing and iteration. Tuples are ordered but immutable, which makes them useful for fixed groups of values.

concepts.title: Sets and dictionaries
concepts.text: Sets store unique hashable values and are ideal for membership tests. Dictionaries map keys to values and work well for structured records such as course scores or user settings.

concepts.title: Comprehensions and built-ins
concepts.text: List, set and dictionary comprehensions offer concise transformations when the expression stays readable. Built-ins such as sum, min, max, sorted, any and all reduce manual looping and often communicate intent more clearly.

codeExample.title: Process learner scores
codeExample.code:
attempts = [
    {"course": "HTML", "score": 95},
    {"course": "JavaScript", "score": 85},
    {"course": "Git", "score": 90},
]

average = sum(item["score"] for item in attempts) / len(attempts)
passed = [item["course"] for item in attempts if item["score"] >= 60]

print(round(average, 1))
print(passed)
explanation: A generator expression supplies values directly to sum.
A list comprehension filters and transforms in one readable step.
The calculation is separate from presentation.

diagram.title: Collection choice
diagram.caption: Choose a collection according to the operations and meaning required by the data.

applications: Lists of courses, dictionaries for profile data and sets of unique skills are common application patterns.
commonMistakes: Using a mutable list/dict as a default argument.
Choosing a list when uniqueness is the real requirement.
Writing deeply nested comprehensions.
Assuming a dictionary key always exists.
bestPractices: Prefer simple comprehensions and normal loops for complex logic.

modules.title: Files & Exceptions
modules.summary: Read files and handle errors with exceptions.
notes: with open(...) automatically closes a file when the block finishes.
Try/except handles expected failures such as invalid input or missing files.
File modes include r for reading, w for writing and a for appending.

concepts.title: Opening files safely
concepts.text: open() creates a file object and accepts modes such as r, w and a. A with statement uses a context manager so the file is closed automatically even if an exception occurs.

concepts.title: Reading and writing text
concepts.text: Text files should normally specify an encoding such as UTF-8. read() can load small files at once, while line-by-line iteration scales better for large files. Writing with mode w replaces existing content, so it should be used carefully.

concepts.title: Exception handling
concepts.text: try contains work that may fail, except handles specific failures, else runs when no exception occurred, and finally runs regardless of the result. Catch only exceptions you can handle meaningfully.

concepts.title: Raising errors
concepts.text: raise allows a function to enforce its contract. For example, invalid score ranges can produce ValueError. Clear error messages make failures easier for callers to diagnose and recover from.

codeExample.title: Read a saved score
explanation: The context manager closes the file automatically.
A missing file and invalid content receive separate handling.
The program recovers with a safe default.

diagram.title: Safe file flow
diagram.caption: Context managers provide deterministic cleanup, while exception handlers deal with recoverable failures.

applications: Exporting a report, reading configuration and processing text files all use these patterns.
commonMistakes: Opening with w and unintentionally erasing content.
Forgetting to close a file.
Using a bare except.
Building paths directly from untrusted input.
bestPractices: Validate data before using or saving it.

modules.title: Relational Database Basics
modules.summary: Understand tables, keys and relationships.
notes: A relational database stores structured data in tables made of rows and columns.
A primary key uniquely identifies each row.
Foreign keys connect related tables and help maintain referential integrity.

concepts.title: Tables, rows and columns
concepts.text: Relational databases store facts in tables. Columns define named attributes and data types, while rows represent individual records. A clear table should represent one entity or relationship and avoid storing several unrelated facts in one field.

concepts.title: Primary keys
concepts.text: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be null. Auto-increment integer IDs are common surrogate keys, while stable natural identifiers can also work when they are truly unique and unlikely to change.

concepts.title: Foreign keys
concepts.text: A foreign key stores the identifier of a related row and can enforce referential integrity. One-to-many relationships place the foreign key on the many side; many-to-many relationships use a junction table that references both entities.

concepts.title: Constraints and normalization
concepts.text: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and foreign-key constraints protect data quality inside the database. Normalization reduces duplication by storing each fact in one logical place, which prevents update anomalies and inconsistent copies.

codeExample.title: Learners and enrollments
explanation: The learner table stores one row per learner.
The enrollment table represents a relationship rather than duplicating learner details.
The composite key prevents duplicate enrollment in the same course.

diagram.title: Relational relationship
diagram.caption: Keys connect independent tables so learner-specific state can be queried without duplicating the same facts repeatedly.

applications: User accounts, enrollments, progress and quiz results are natural relational records in SkillForge.
commonMistakes: Using names as primary keys.
Storing comma-separated IDs in one column.
Duplicating user details in every enrollment row.
Using mismatched data types for related keys.
bestPractices: Normalize enough to avoid duplicated facts.

modules.title: SQL CRUD Operations
modules.summary: Create, read, update and delete data with SQL.
notes: INSERT adds rows, SELECT reads rows, UPDATE changes rows and DELETE removes rows.
WHERE filters rows and ORDER BY controls result ordering.
Parameterized queries should be used in applications to reduce SQL injection risk.

concepts.title: Create with INSERT
concepts.text: INSERT adds rows. Listing the target columns makes a statement explicit and prevents accidental dependence on physical column order. Auto-generated IDs are usually omitted so the database can assign them.

concepts.title: Read with SELECT
concepts.text: SELECT retrieves data. WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY controls sorting, LIMIT constrains result count and aggregate functions such as COUNT and AVG summarize groups of records.

concepts.title: Update safely
concepts.text: UPDATE changes existing rows. A missing WHERE clause can modify an entire table, so the target condition should be tested carefully. Applications should also verify that a learner is authorized to change the selected record.

concepts.title: Delete and parameterization
concepts.text: DELETE removes rows and carries the same WHERE-clause risk as UPDATE. In application code, external values should be passed as query parameters rather than concatenated into SQL strings; this keeps data separate from SQL syntax and prevents injection.

codeExample.title: CRUD examples
explanation: Each statement maps to one CRUD operation.
The UPDATE and DELETE statements deliberately target one row.
Application code should parameterize all external values rather than embedding them directly.

diagram.title: CRUD lifecycle
diagram.caption: CRUD is the foundation of most database-backed web application workflows.

applications: Registration creates users, dashboards read state, profile screens update records and account-cleanup workflows may delete data.
commonMistakes: Running UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE.
Concatenating form input into SQL.
Using = NULL instead of IS NULL.
Selecting unnecessary columns everywhere.

modules.title: Joins & Design
modules.summary: Combine related tables and apply normalization basics.
notes: INNER JOIN returns matching rows from related tables.
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table even when no match exists.
Normalization reduces unnecessary duplication and update anomalies.

concepts.title: INNER JOIN
concepts.text: INNER JOIN returns rows where the join condition matches on both tables. It is the right choice when a result only makes sense if both related records exist.

concepts.title: LEFT JOIN
concepts.text: LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left table and fills right-side columns with NULL when no match exists. This is useful for reports such as 'all users, including those with no quiz attempts'.

concepts.title: Joining several relationships
concepts.text: Queries can join several tables, but developers must understand cardinality because one-to-many joins multiply rows. Aggregation with GROUP BY can then collapse those rows into one result per learner or course.

concepts.title: Schema design and normalization
concepts.text: Good joins depend on sound relationships. Stable IDs, foreign keys and normalized tables make queries predictable. Denormalization can be useful in specialized performance cases, but it should be a measured trade-off rather than the default.

codeExample.title: Attempt count per learner
codeExample.code:
SELECT u.id,
       u.name,
       COUNT(q.id) AS attempts
FROM users AS u
LEFT JOIN quiz_results AS q
    ON q.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name
ORDER BY attempts DESC;
explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps learners with zero attempts.
COUNT(q.id) counts only matching quiz rows.
GROUP BY returns one summary row per learner.

diagram.title: Join path
diagram.caption: Joins follow shared keys; understanding those relationships is more reliable than joining by display text such as names.

applications: Report cards and admin summaries frequently combine learner identity with enrollments, progress and results.
commonMistakes: Joining on names instead of IDs.
Putting right-table filters in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN and removing unmatched rows.
Ignoring row multiplication.
Duplicating entity data into relationship tables.
bestPractices: Inspect raw rows before GROUP BY.
Index frequently joined/filter columns when needed.

modules.title: Grouping and Aggregate Queries
modules.summary: Practice grouping and aggregate queries through a worked example and a short verification exercise.
notes: COUNT counts rows, SUM totals numeric values and AVG computes their average.
GROUP BY calculates aggregates separately for each group, such as course_id.
WHERE filters source rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the grouped results.

concepts.title: Core idea
concepts.text: COUNT counts rows, SUM totals numeric values and AVG computes their average.

concepts.title: Putting it into practice
concepts.text: GROUP BY calculates aggregates separately for each group, such as course_id.

concepts.title: Checking the result
concepts.text: WHERE filters source rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the grouped results.

codeExample.title: Worked example
codeExample.code:
SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS learners
FROM enrollments
GROUP BY course_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5;
-- Shows only courses with five or more enrollments.
explanation: COUNT counts rows, SUM totals numeric values and AVG computes their average.
WHERE filters source rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the grouped results.

bestPractices: WHERE filters source rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the grouped results.
